newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel to study Hapoalim asset sales.
newsitem.headline: Israel to study Hapoalim asset sales.

text.p: The Israeli government will investigate the legal ramifications of forcing Bank Hapoalim to sell its holdings in both Koor Industries and Clal Israel, the Treasury said on Monday.

A spokesman said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had ordered the study, to be completed in two weeks, after a meeting today with officials from the Finance and Justice Ministries, the Bank of Israel and outside advisers.
Hapoalim holds 22.7 percent of Koor and 30.5 percent of Clal.

Under existing bank reform legislation Hapoalim is required to divest its holdings in one of the two holding companies. Like other commercial banks, Hapoalim was also forced last year to reduce its holding in non-bank companies to a ceiling of 25 percent.
However, Netanyahu's chief economic adviser, Moshe Leon, said two weeks ago he wanted to force Hapoalim to divest itself of both Koor and Clal, Israel's two biggest holding companies.
Leon also said he also wanted Hapoalim to sell off its small-bank subsidiaries, but at today's meeting that proposal was not discussed.

The Treasury spokesman indicated that the ministry supports the divestiture plan under study, saying it is a natural extension of the earliest bank reform. Bank of Israel officials have said in the past they are opposed because it would hinder Hapoalim's prospective sale.

Hapoalim is one of the "arrangement" banks, which were acquired by the government in exchange for bailing out shareholders after the 1983 bank shares crash. The government owns 77 percent of the bank.

The government published a tender in 1994 to sell a controlling stake in Hapoalim, but last year one of the two groups bidding for the bank dropped out after the bank reform legislation stripped Hapoalim of much its non-bank assets.
In the last few weeks, a new group centred on the U.S. banker Jeffrey Keil, has reportedly been formed to make a bid.
